translations.text: A discourse by the same John Chrysostom. From the commentary on the Gospel
according to Matthew. On the ten virgins and the talents, delivered on Holy Tuesday.
Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps
and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride. Five of them were wise,
and five were foolish. The foolish ones took no oil in their vessels.
Then, while the bridegroom delayed, they all grew drowsy and slept. At midnight there was a cry:
“Look, the bridegroom is coming! Go out to meet him.” They rose, and, being short
of supplies, five of them said to the wise ones, “Give us some of your oil too.”
But the wise ones would not listen, saying, “There may not be enough for you and us.
Go to the sellers and buy some.” While they were going for this purpose, the bridegroom came, and the others went in.
Those who came afterward said, “Open the door for us too.” But he said, “Truly I tell you, I do not know you.”
Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day. Then he told another parable: Again, a man going away called his servants
and gave them his property: to one, five talents; to another, two; and to another, one,
to each according to his own ability. And he went away. Then the two brought back twice as much, but the one who had received one
brought back that one. When called to account, he said, “I knew that you were a hard man,
reaping where you have not sown and gathering where you have not scattered.
So I was afraid and hid your talent. Here is what belongs to you.”
His master answered him, “You deceitful and lazy servant!
If you knew that I reap where I have not sown and gather where I have not scattered,
you should have given my money to those who trade with it, and when I returned,
I would have received what was mine with interest. Therefore take the talent from him
and give it to the one who has ten talents. For everyone who has will always be given more, and he will have an abundance.
But from the one who does not have, even what he thinks he has will be taken away.
And throw the useless servant into the outer darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”
These parables resemble the one about the faithful servant and the foolish servant who squandered his master's property.
For there are four in all, telling us about this in different ways—I mean compassionate assistance.
And we must help our neighbor in every way we can, since it is impossible to be saved otherwise.
Here, then, he speaks about every kind of assistance
that we ought to give our neighbor; but in the parable of the virgins he speaks specifically about mercy,
which, he says, is shown through possessions, and much more strongly than in the first parable.
For there he punishes the man who beats others, gets drunk, and squanders and wastes his master's possessions.
But here he also punishes the one who does not put his possessions to good use and [?] generously distributes his possessions to those in need.
For they had oil, but not enough; therefore they too are punished. But why does he introduce the figures of virgins into the parable,
and not simply [?]? For why does he introduce
such a character? He spoke highly of virginity, saying, “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.
Let whoever can accept this accept it.” He also knows that many people hold them in great
esteem. For [?] it is by nature a great deed. And he shows that not even among the people of old
was it accomplished by those first holy men. Nor did he make it compulsory in the new covenant; likewise, the Law did not command it,
but he left it to the choice of his hearers. Therefore Paul also said, “I impose no compulsion, nor [?] on anyone who wishes,
nor do I give a command about this matter.” Since, then, it was a great deed
and was held in great esteem by many, so that no one who had accomplished this
might become careless about the rest, as though he had accomplished everything,
he presents this parable, sufficient to convince us that even if virginity possesses everything else,
if it lacks the good things that come from mercy, it will be cast out with the sexually immoral and the foolish.
And he will place them with those people without mercy. For they overcame bodily desire, but they did not overcome the desire for possessions.
For bodily desire is not equal to the desire for possessions; rather, bodily desire is more violent and harder to overcome.
The weaker the opponent, the less excuse there is for those who are defeated. For this reason
he also calls them foolish: they endured the greater struggle, but lost everything because of the lesser one.
By the lamps here he meant the gift of virginity, holy purity; and by the oil, help for those in need.
“While the bridegroom delayed, they all grew drowsy and slept.” He shows that his coming again will not be after a short time.
In the meantime, drawing the disciples away from expecting his kingdom to appear fully at that very time.
For that was all they hoped for. For this reason he firmly restrains them from that hope. After this he also shows
that death is sleep. For he said, “They were sleeping, and at midnight there was a cry.”
Either this refers to the parable, or else it shows that the resurrection will take place at night.
Paul also speaks of a cry, saying, “At a command and at the voice of an archangel,
at the last trumpet blast, he will come down from heaven.” What do the trumpets mean, and what does the cry mean?
He says, “The bridegroom is coming.” And when they had put their lamps in order,
the foolish ones said to the wise, “Give us some of your oil.” Again he calls them foolish, showing that no one is more foolish
than someone who gathers wealth here and goes away naked to that place where we especially need compassion,
where greater mercy is needed. They are foolish not only for this reason, but also because they hoped
to receive some from the others and asked at the wrong time. Yet no one was more compassionate than those virgins.
For this reason they were all the more kindly disposed. And they do not ask for all of it, for they said, “Give us some of your oil.”
They also show how urgent their need is, for they said, “Our lamps are going out.”
But even so they did not receive any. For neither the compassion of those whom they were asking,
nor the modesty of their request, nor its urgency and necessity enabled them to obtain it.
What, then, do we learn from this? Is it not that no one can defend any of us there if our deeds have condemned us?
Since they cannot, they also direct you toward what is impossible [?]. Blessed Abraham also made this known when he said:
“There is a chasm between you and us, so that those who wish to cross cannot pass over.”
“Go to those who sell and buy some.” And who are those who sell? The poor. And where are they? Here.
You should have asked, not at that hour. Do you see how great a gain comes to us from the poor?
If you lose this, you have lost a great hope of our salvation. Therefore it is here that we must
gather oil, so that it may be available for use there when the hour calls us.
For that is not the time for us to gather it. So do not waste your possessions pointlessly on food and vanity, for you will have great need of mercy there.
When those women heard this, they went away, but accomplished nothing. He said this either in telling the parable
and [?] it, or to show that even if we become compassionate after death,
We will gain nothing from this toward escaping. Therefore, mere advice was not enough for them either.
For they did not go to the sellers here, but there. Nor did it help the rich man, who became so concerned for others
that he even cared for those connected with him. For he who had passed by the man lying at his gates
wants to rescue from misery and [?] those whom he had not even seen, and begs that some people be sent
to tell them these things. Nevertheless, he gained nothing from this, just as these women did not.
For after they heard this and went away, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him.
But the others were shut outside, after great and unspeakable labors,
sweat, and that fierce battle raging against nature, and the victories they had won.
Disgraced, with their lamps extinguished, they went away with their heads bowed. For nothing is darker than virginity
without oil, which is mercy. For this is also why many people commonly call the merciless dark.
What benefit, then, did they gain from virginity, when they did not see the bridegroom?
Nor did they succeed by knocking. Instead, they heard those fearful words: “Go away;
I do not know you.” And when he himself says this, there is nothing else
except [?] and unbearable torment. Those words are harsher than [?].
And to those who practice lawlessness he said, “Keep watch, therefore, for you do not know the day or the hour.”
Do you see how often he mentions this, showing that mercy is necessary?
There are some who are idle throughout their lives, but when we rebuke them, they say,
“At the hour of death I will leave something to those in need.”
Let them hear these words and mend their ways. For many have failed to do this, being suddenly snatched away at that hour,
without even being allowed to arrange their own affairs as they wished. This parable, then, was spoken about mercy
shown through possessions; but the one that follows also concerns those who do not wish, through wealth, words,
protection, or anything else, to be of benefit to their neighbor,
but hide everything away. Why, then, does that parable introduce a king, while this one introduces a bridegroom?
So that you may learn how much care Christ has for virgins who distribute what they possess—that is, their virginity.
Therefore Paul, too, lays down this rule concerning the matter: “The unmarried woman cares about the Lord,” he said, and about what is proper.
and undistracted devotion to the Lord. “Thus we pray,” he said. In Luke, however, the parable of the talents is presented differently.
This means, then, that this is one thing and that is another. For in one of them, from a single sum [?],
different returns were produced from a single mina: one brought five, and the other ten.
Therefore they did not receive the same reward. But here it is otherwise. For this reason the crown is also the same.
For the man who received two added two, and the man who received five did likewise. But there, since from the same initial deposit
one produced a greater return and the other a smaller one, it is fitting that they should also receive unequal prizes in the contests.
Notice how everywhere he does not demand an accounting immediately. For [?] in the case of the vineyard too, he handed it over to the workers and went away.
Here too, after entrusting his property to them, he went away, so that you might recognize his patience.
It seems to me that he says this also to indicate the resurrection. But here there are no longer workers and a vineyard; rather, you are the workers.
For he speaks not only to the rulers and the Jews, but to everyone.
And those who bring their returns wisely acknowledge both their own part and their master’s. One says, “You gave me five talents,” and the other also speaks, showing
that they had received from him the starting point for their work, and much grace
was theirs, and they consider everything they have to come from him.
What, then, does the master say? “Well done, good servant,” he said. For this is the mark of a good person: caring for one’s neighbor.
“Faithful servant, you were faithful over a little; I will put you in charge of much. Enter into the joy
of your master.” With these words he showed the fullness of blessedness. But the other did not speak this way. How did he speak? “I knew that you are a hard man,
reaping where you did not sow and gathering where you did not scatter.
And I was afraid and hid your talent. Here, you have what is yours.”
What, then, does the master say? “You ought to have deposited my money with the bankers.” That is, you ought to have spoken, urged,
and offered advice. “But what if they do not listen?” That is not your concern. What could be easier than this? For people do not act this way,
but require the lender himself to press for repayment and demand it. “But you ought to have deposited it,” he said,
“and left the collection to me. Then I would have collected it with interest.”
By interest he means obedience demonstrated in deeds. It would have been easier for you to show this and do it,
and leave the harder task to me. But since you did not do this,
“Take the talent away from him,” he said, “and give it to the one who has ten talents.”
For to the one who has, more will be given everywhere, and he will have an abundance.
But from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away.
What does this mean? Someone who has the gift of speech for teaching, but does not put it to use,
will lose even the gift. For the one who makes progress receives a greater gift.
For that is how he loses what he received. But the idle person suffers not only this loss, but also unbearable
torment, and after the torment, a judgment filled with many reproaches.
For he said, “Throw the useless servant into the outer darkness. There is weeping and gnashing of teeth.”
Do you see that it is not only the robber and the greedy person, nor only those who do evil,
but also the one who does not do good who suffers the ultimate torment? Let us therefore listen to these words while there is still time.
Let us secure our salvation. Let us obtain oil for our lamps. Let us put our talent to work.
But if we grow lazy and go about idly here, no one will have mercy on us
there, even if we weep greatly for our sins. The man who had filthy clothes gained nothing either.
The man entrusted with one talent returned it, yet even so he was condemned.
The virgins pleaded, came, and knocked, but it was all in vain and senseless. Knowing this, then,
let us offer everything for the benefit of our neighbors. For the talents here are each person's abilities,
whether in giving protection, in possessions, in teaching, or in any service
of this kind. Let no one say, “I have only one talent and can do nothing.”
You can do good even with one. For you are no poorer than that widow.
You are no more ignorant than Peter and John, who were ignorant and uneducated.
Nevertheless, because they showed zeal and did everything for the common good,
they gained heaven. For nothing is so pleasing to God as living for the common good.
For this reason God has given us speech, hands, feet, and bodily strength,
as well as a mind and understanding, so that we may devote all these to our salvation and to the benefit of our neighbors.
For we need speech not only for praise and thanksgiving, but also for effective teaching and encouragement.
If we use it for this, we will be imitators of the Master; but if we use it for the opposite, we will be imitators of the devil.
For Peter too, when he confessed Christ, was called blessed, as one who had proclaimed what came from the Father.
But when he rejected the cross and argued against it, he was rebuked very severely,
as one thinking the devil’s thoughts. If, then, so severe a rebuke was spoken to him when he acted in ignorance, when we sin deliberately,
how shall we receive forgiveness? This, then, is what we now say, so that it may be clear from this that the words are Christ’s.
For it is not only if I say, “Rise and walk,” or if I say, “Tabitha, arise,” that I speak his words.
Rather, he spoke to many: if I am reviled, I will bless; if I suffer harm, I will pray for the one who harmed me.
Earlier, then, I said that our tongue is a hand touching Christ’s foot. But now I say something much greater:
that our tongue is a tongue imitating Christ’s tongue, if
it is fitting to say so. Careful examination will show this, if we say what he wishes.
And what is it that he wishes us to do? To speak words full of calmness and gentleness,
just as he himself spoke, saying to those who reviled him, “I do not have a demon.”
And again, “If I have spoken wrongly, testify to the wrong.” If you too speak this way,
if you speak to set your neighbor right, you will acquire a tongue like his.
And God himself said this: “For whoever brings forth what is precious from what is worthless
shall be as my mouth.” When, therefore, your tongue becomes like Christ’s tongue,
your mouth will also become like the Father’s mouth, and you will be a temple of the Holy Spirit.
What honor, then, could equal this? For even if your mouth were fashioned from gold
and precious stones, it would not shine so brightly
as it does now, lit up by the adornment of gentleness. For what is lovelier than a mouth that does not know how to revile,
but practices blessing? But if you cannot bless the person who curses you,
keep silent; accomplish at least that. And by traveling along the road and hastening as you should,
you will reach that point too, and make your mouth such as we have described. And do not think that what has been said is audacious.
For the Master loves humankind, and this is a gift of his goodness. What is audacious is to have a mouth like the devil’s
mouth, and likewise to make your tongue like that of a crafty demon—especially when you receive such mysteries
and partake of that very flesh of the Lord. Keeping this in mind, then, remain in him as far as you are able.
Then he cannot even look at you once you have become like this.
For does he not recognize the king’s image and know Christ’s weapons, by which he was defeated?
And what are these weapons? Gentleness and meekness. For [?], when he approached him on the mountain, he provoked him and went on speaking.
He did not know [?] that he was Christ. But with those words Christ struck him through gentleness; through gentleness he won the victory.
Do the same yourself. If you see someone who has made himself a devil coming toward you,
you too must overcome him in the same way. Christ has given you the power to be like him,
as far as your strength allows. Do not be afraid when you hear this, for what is frightening is not to be like him.
Speak, then, as he does, and in this respect you will be as he is. For this reason, greater is the one
who speaks in this way than the one who prophesies. For the latter has everything as a gift, but here there is also your own labor and sweat.
Teach your soul to make your mouth like Christ’s mouth. For it can do this if it wishes.
It knows this art, provided it is not lazy. “And how,” someone says, “is such a mouth fashioned? With what colors? With what material?” With nothing
except goodness alone, gentleness, and humility.
Let us also see how mouths become the devil’s, so that we never make ours like that.
How, then, is such a mouth fashioned? Through oaths, blasphemies, incantations, and envy. For whenever someone speaks these things,
he takes on the devil’s tongue. How, then, shall we receive forgiveness? Rather, what punishment shall we not undergo,
since the tongue with which we were counted worthy to taste the Lord’s flesh—
we look on as it speaks the devil’s words! Let us not, then, look on at this,
but make every effort to teach it to imitate its Lord.
For if we learn this, it will give us great confidence when we stand before Christ’s judgment seat. For if anyone does not know how to speak in this way,
the Judge will not listen to him. For just as, when the judge happens to be a Roman,
he does not listen to someone making a defense who cannot speak his language, so it is with Christ.
If you do not speak as he does, he will not listen to you or pay attention. Let us therefore learn to speak
as our King is accustomed to hearing. Let us strive to imitate his way of speaking.
Even if you fall into grief, take care that the pain of sorrow does not turn your mouth aside,
but speak as Christ did. For he too mourned for Lazarus and Judas. And even if you fall into fear,
you will fall. Learn to speak again as he did. For he too fell into fear for your sake, in accordance with his wise plan.
You too should say, “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” Even if you weep, shed your tears quietly,
as he did. Even if you fall into trials—for [?] he too experiences trials and is sorrowful and says,
“My soul is deeply sorrowful, even to death.” And he gives you all these examples so that you may observe moderation
and [?] the guidance given to you. In this way you will be able to have a mouth like his mouth.
In this way, while walking on earth, you will show us the tongue of the one seated on high, observing the same moderation in sorrow and in anger,
in mourning and in toil. How many of you think of seeing his image
only! Yet it is even possible to become like him, if we make the effort. So let us not hold back.
For he does not welcome the mouths of prophets so much as those of meek and gentle people.
For he said, “Many will say to me, ‘We prophesied in your name,’ and I will say to them, ‘I never knew you.’”
But he welcomed Moses’ mouth because he was meek and gentle. For it says, “The man Moses was meeker than all the people
on earth.” He was so welcomed and loved that God spoke with him face to face
and mouth to mouth, as a friend speaks to his friend.
Do you not rebuke demons now? Yet then you will rebuke the nature
of fire. If your mouth is like Christ’s mouth, you will rebuke the fiery abyss
and say, “Be silent! Turn back!” And with great confidence you will ascend to heaven and be filled with the kingdom.
May we all attain it through the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ,
with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.
